chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Business Cycle, Explained for Investors

lessons.title: India's Business Cycles Since 2003: From the Capex Boom to the Post-Covid Revival

body.text: India's cycles are not identical, but they rhyme. A credit and capex boom overreaches, something breaks, balance sheets take years to repair, and the next upcycle starts only once that repair is done.

children.text: Lesson 1.1 gave you the four phases in the abstract. This lesson gives you the actual history, because you cannot judge where India is today without knowing where it has been. Every major Indian cycle since 2003 left fingerprints on specific sectors, and those fingerprints are exactly what Chapters 3 and 4 will use to test sector rotation on real NSE data.
Two Decades of Growth, in One Chart

body.title: India real GDP growth by fiscal year (%)

children.text: Three things jump out. First, the long run of roughly 8% growth from FY04 to FY08. Second, the three deep troughs: FY09 (the global financial crisis), FY20 and FY21 (the NBFC slowdown followed by Covid). Third, the shallower, grinding dip of FY12 and FY13, which never looked dramatic on a chart but hurt investors badly. A cycle does not need a negative number to wreck portfolios.

body.text: Handle the numbers in this chart with care. They come from the World Bank's series for India, which is built from official data but stitches together different base years. India's official GDP series has been rebased several times, most recently in February 2026 to base year 2022-23, and MoSPI plans to release a revised back series. Growth for any individual year, especially FY09 and FY23 onwards, may look different depending on which vintage you consult. Use the chart for the shape of the cycle, not for decimal precision.

children.text: The Seven Episodes

events.title: The capex and credit boom
events.description: Growth runs near 8% or above for five years. Bank credit grows about 30% a year on average from FY05 to FY07, investment hits roughly 36% of GDP, and the Nifty rises about sevenfold.

events.title: Global financial crisis
events.description: Lehman Brothers collapses in September 2008. Foreign money flees, the Nifty falls about 60% from its January 2008 peak, and FY09 growth drops sharply. The RBI cuts the repo rate from 9% to 4.75% by April 2009.

events.title: V-shaped recovery, then inflation
events.description: Stimulus and rate cuts produce a fast rebound, but inflation follows. From March 2010 to October 2011 the RBI raises the repo rate from 4.75% to 8.5%.

events.title: The long slowdown
events.description: Stalled projects, policy paralysis, high inflation, and overleveraged companies drag growth down. The 2013 taper tantrum sends the rupee to a then record low of 68.85 per dollar on 28 August 2013.

events.title: Clean-up and shocks
events.description: Falling crude helps, but banks confront their bad loans after the RBI's Asset Quality Review of 2015. Demonetisation in 2016, GST in 2017, and the IL&FS defaults of 2018 interrupt growth, which slides to 3.9% in FY20.

events.title: Covid contraction, then a government-led upcycle
events.description: The lockdown produces India's first annual contraction since 1979-80. Recovery follows on the back of low rates, repaired bank balance sheets, and a sharp rise in central government capex.

events.title: Soft patch and easing
events.description: Earnings growth cools, the Nifty corrects about 16% from its September 2024 record, and the RBI cuts the repo rate from 6.5% to 5.25% during 2025. Growth holds up in the new GDP series.

children.text: Episode 1: The Capex and Credit Boom (2003 to 2008)

markDefs.definition: Projects such as roads, airports, and power plants where a private company builds and operates an asset under a contract with the government, usually financed heavily by bank loans and repaid from future user charges or tariffs.

children.text: This was India's great investment boom. Companies built steel plants, power stations, ports, and telecom networks, and banks funded them enthusiastically. Infrastructure projects were often structured as
public-private partnerships
, financed with long term bank loans against revenue that was still years away. Capital goods, infrastructure, real estate, metals, and banks led the market. It felt permanent. It was not.

stats.label: Nifty, Apr 2003 to Jan 2008
stats.context: About 6.8 times in under five years

stats.label: Fixed investment, FY08
stats.context: Peak of the boom, on the older GDP series

stats.label: RBI repo rate, Jul 2008
stats.context: The RBI tightened as the boom overheated

body.text: The seeds of the next decade's pain were planted in the best years. Loans made to power and infrastructure projects between 2005 and 2010 became a large share of the bad loans banks were still cleaning up in 2016 to 2018. When credit grows 30% a year, underwriting standards almost always slip.

children.text: Episode 2: The Global Financial Crisis (2008 to 2009)

India did not have a subprime problem, but it was far more connected to global money than it had been a decade earlier. When Lehman Brothers failed in September 2008, foreign investors pulled out, credit markets froze, and export demand collapsed. The Nifty fell from an intraday peak of 6,357 in January 2008 to a close of 2,524 on 27 October 2008, a fall of about 60%.

body.label: RBI response speed
body.value: 425 bps of repo cuts in about nine months
body.context: From 9% in October 2008 to 4.75% by April 2009, alongside cuts to the cash reserve ratio and a government fiscal stimulus

children.text: Episode 3: V-Shaped Recovery, Then Inflation (2009 to 2011)

The policy response worked, almost too well. Growth bounced back quickly, and the Nifty roughly doubled off its lows by the end of 2009. But the combination of stimulus, food price spikes, and rising crude pushed inflation well into high single digits. The RBI reversed course hard, lifting the repo rate by a cumulative 375 basis points between March 2010 and October 2011. Rate sensitive sectors that had led the recovery lost leadership as rates climbed.
Episode 4: The Long Slowdown (2011 to 2014)

markDefs.definition: A situation where both overleveraged companies and the banks that lent to them have damaged balance sheets at the same time. Stressed companies cannot invest, and stressed banks cannot lend, so each keeps the other weak.

children.text: This is the episode investors underestimate because GDP never contracted. Big projects stalled on land, environment, and fuel supply approvals. Companies that had borrowed heavily in the boom could not service their debt, and their lenders, mostly public sector banks, were stuck with the loans. The Economic Survey of 2016-17 later called this the
twin balance sheet problem
. Add high inflation and a widening current account deficit, and India was badly exposed when the US Federal Reserve signalled in 2013 that it would taper its bond buying.

The Nifty fell about 28% from its November 2010 peak to its December 2011 low, and the rupee hit 68.85 per dollar on 28 August 2013. Infrastructure, capital goods, real estate, and PSU bank stocks, the heroes of 2003 to 2008, were the worst hit. Consumer staples, pharma, and IT services, businesses with low debt and export or defensive demand, held up far better.
Episode 5: Clean-Up and Shocks (2014 to 2019)

Crude oil prices collapsed from mid 2014, cutting India's import bill and inflation. But the bad loans could no longer be hidden. The RBI's Asset Quality Review in 2015 forced banks to recognise stressed loans, and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code of 2016 created a way to resolve them. Gross NPAs of scheduled commercial banks climbed above 11% by March 2018. Private investment stayed weak throughout.

Then came three shocks in quick succession: demonetisation in November 2016, the GST rollout in July 2017, and the IL&FS defaults in September 2018 that froze NBFC funding. Growth slid to 3.9% in FY20, before Covid had even arrived. Investors crowded into a narrow set of high quality consumer and private financial companies, leaving most of the market behind.
Episode 6: Covid Contraction, Then a Government-Led Upcycle (2020 to 2024)

You saw the contraction phase in Lesson 1.1. What makes the recovery that followed different from 2003 to 2008 is who led it. Private companies were cautious, so the central government stepped up with a sharp rise in its own capital spending on roads, railways, and defence. Meanwhile, the bad loan clean-up of the previous five years meant banks entered this cycle with the strongest balance sheets in over a decade.

stats.label: RBI repo rate, Feb 2023
stats.context: Up from 4% in May 2022 as inflation rose

children.text: Episode 7: Soft Patch and Easing (2024 to 2026)

By late 2024, corporate earnings growth had cooled and valuations were stretched. The Nifty fell from its record of 26,277.35 on 27 September 2024 to 21,964.60 on 4 March 2025, a drop of about 16%, and it closed lower for five straight months from October 2024 to February 2025. With inflation easing, the RBI cut the repo rate from 6.5% to 5.25% over the course of 2025. It then held rates at 5.25% through its August 2026 meeting, citing global uncertainty.

body.text: Be careful about labelling the most recent phase. At the time of writing, the data is still being revised, the new GDP series has no full back history yet, and the RBI has paused. Whether 2024 to 2025 was a mid-cycle soft patch or the start of a deeper slowdown will only be clear in hindsight. Chapter 2 gives you the tools to form your own view as new data arrives.

children.text: The RBI Rate Cycle Across Two Decades

body.title: RBI repo rate at key turning points (%)

children.text: These are turning points only, not every change, so the spacing on the axis is not proportional to time. The pattern is still clear: the RBI cuts hard in contractions, tightens once recovery turns into inflation, and eases again when growth softens. Lesson 2.3 turns this into a timing tool.

body.text: The sector leadership columns are broad, simplified summaries for teaching purposes. Leadership within each episode shifted over time and varied across individual stocks. Chapter 4 tests these patterns properly against Nifty sectoral index data.

body.title: The 2003 to 2008 Boom vs the 2021 to 2024 Upcycle

columns.label: 2003 to 2008
points: Funded by bank credit growing about 30% a year
Many companies took on heavy debt
Banks entered the boom lending aggressively and exited with a pipeline of future bad loans

columns.label: 2021 to 2024
points: Led by central government capex, with private capex slower to follow
Credit growth strong but from much cleaner balance sheets
Large companies had spent the 2010s cutting debt
Banks entered the cycle with gross NPAs falling towards multi-year lows

body.title: Go deeper: why the credit cycle keeps repeating

children.text: Look back across the episodes and one engine shows up every time: credit.
In the boom, strong growth makes borrowers look safe, so lenders relax standards and lend more. More lending funds more investment, which boosts growth further.
When growth slows or rates rise, the weakest borrowers default first. Lenders pull back, which slows growth more and exposes the next layer of weak borrowers.
Recognising and resolving those bad loans takes years, not quarters. Between 2015 and 2018, banks did the painful recognition; the payoff in clean balance sheets arrived only in 2021 to 2024.
Only once banks are healthy and companies have deleveraged does the next credit upcycle begin. That is why bank credit growth and gross NPA trends appear in the cycle dashboard in Lesson 2.2.
Practice

body.title: Size the Boom
body.prompt: The Nifty was at about 930 in late April 2003 and hit an intraday peak of 6,357 in January 2008. What was the percentage gain from 930 to 6,357? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (6,357 divided by 930) minus 1, multiplied by 100, gives about 583.5%. The index rose roughly 6.8 times in under five years. Then it gave back about 60% in ten months. Leadership concentrated in cyclical sectors magnified both legs.

body.title: Measure the Policy Swing
body.prompt: The RBI cut the repo rate from 9% to 4.75% during the global financial crisis, and then raised it to 8.5% by October 2011. How many basis points did the repo rate rise between the April 2009 low and October 2011?
body.explanation: 8.5% minus 4.75% is 3.75 percentage points, which is 375 basis points (one percentage point is 100 basis points). A tightening of that size in under two years is a big reason rate sensitive sectors lost leadership as the recovery turned into the 2011 to 2014 slowdown.

body.title: Name the Problem
body.textWithBlank: When both overleveraged companies and the banks that lent to them are stressed at the same time, so that neither can invest or lend, the Economic Survey of 2016-17 called it the ___ problem.
body.explanation: The twin balance sheet problem explains why India's slowdown after 2011 lasted so long. Stressed borrowers could not invest, and stressed banks could not lend, so private capex stayed weak for most of the decade.

body.title: Spot the Difference
body.question: Which feature most clearly separates the 2021 to 2024 upcycle from the 2003 to 2008 boom?
options: The 2021 to 2024 upcycle had no role for bank credit at all
The 2021 to 2024 upcycle was led by government capex and started with much healthier bank and corporate balance sheets
The 2003 to 2008 boom happened while the RBI was cutting rates continuously
The 2003 to 2008 boom was led by FMCG and IT services
body.explanation: The 2003 to 2008 boom was driven by private capex funded by roughly 30% annual credit growth, which left a pile of future bad loans. The 2021 to 2024 upcycle leaned on central government capex, and it started after banks had cleaned up their NPAs and large companies had cut debt. Credit still grew strongly, and the RBI was hiking, not cutting, through much of the 2003 to 2008 period.

body.title: Learn From 2011
body.scenario: It is 2026. A friend has built a portfolio heavy in capital goods, infrastructure, and PSU bank stocks after watching them lead the market from 2021 to 2024. They say: "The government is spending, India is growing at over 7%, these sectors can only keep winning."
body.prompt: Using the 2003 to 2008 boom and the 2011 to 2014 slowdown as reference points, what questions should your friend ask before assuming the leadership continues?
body.modelAnswer: Leadership in 2003 to 2008 also felt permanent, and the same sectors were the worst performers from 2011 to 2014. Your friend should ask a few things. First, is growth broadening into private capex, or is it still dependent on government spending, which is limited by the fiscal deficit? Second, are credit growth and leverage at these companies rising fast enough to repeat the old mistake, or are balance sheets still clean? Third, what is the RBI doing? A pause or hiking cycle hurts rate sensitive sectors. Fourth, how much of the good news is already in valuations after a multi-year run? Strong GDP growth does not by itself protect sectors whose earnings and valuations already assume it will continue. None of this means the sectors must fall, but it means concentration should be a deliberate, sized decision, not an extrapolation.

body.label: RBI Database on Indian Economy (DBIE)
body.description: The RBI's official data portal. Free historical series for the policy repo rate, bank credit growth, inflation, and exchange rates used to trace every episode in this lesson.

body.text: This lesson is a historical and educational overview. It is not investment advice or a recommendation about any sector, stock, or fund. Past cycles and past sector leadership do not guarantee future outcomes.

points: India has passed through seven distinct cycle episodes since 2003, each with different leading and lagging sectors
2003 to 2008 was a private capex and credit boom: bank credit grew about 30% a year and the Nifty rose from about 930 to 6,357
The global financial crisis cut the Nifty by about 60%, and the RBI slashed the repo rate by 425 bps to 4.75% in about nine months
The 2011 to 2014 slowdown never produced negative GDP growth, but stalled projects and twin balance sheets hurt the boom's favourite sectors badly
The 2014 to 2019 clean-up pushed bank gross NPAs above 11% before recovery; the payoff came in the 2021 to 2024 upcycle led by government capex
The same credit cycle engine repeats: boom, bad loans, years of repair, then a new upcycle once balance sheets are healthy
Treat recent phases, including 2024 to 2026, as provisional calls, especially while India's new GDP series awaits a full back history
